Nigeria's 36 states are mostly named after a river, a city or a people,
and the states were carved up repeatedly (1967, 1976, 1987, 1991, 1996)
to break the three big regions apart - so many names are recent
coinages over much older kingdoms: Sokoto and Kano are Hausa emirates,
Oyo and Benin were Yoruba and Edo empires, Borno was Kanem-Bornu.
Several etymologies here are genuinely contested in the sources, and
the sentence says so where that is the case rather than picking one.
The country's own name is from the Niger, a river whose name is
probably Tuareg n'ger-n-gereo, 'river of rivers', not Latin niger.
sokoto: From Arabic suq, a market — the Hausa rendering of the name of the caliphate's capital.
The Sokoto Caliphate, founded by Usman dan Fodio in 1804, was the largest state in Africa in the nineteenth century.
Its Sultan is still the most senior Muslim authority in Nigeria, and the state is the hottest part of the country.
katsina: Named for the city, said to be after Katsina, the wife of a local ruler.
One of the seven original Hausa city-states, and a centre of Islamic learning that rivalled Timbuktu in the 1500s.
Its Gobarau minaret, built of mud in the fifteenth century, is one of the oldest surviving structures in West Africa.
zamfara: Named for the Zamfarawa, a Hausa subgroup, and their old kingdom.
In 1999 it became the first Nigerian state to adopt sharia criminal law, and eleven others followed.
Artisanal gold mining here caused one of the worst lead-poisoning episodes ever recorded, in 2010.
yobe: Named for the Yobe river, which forms part of the border with Niger.
It was split from Borno in 1991, so it shares the Kanuri history of the old Bornu empire.
Much of it is Sahel scrub, and the Hadejia-Nguru wetlands on its edge are a vital stop for birds crossing the Sahara.
kebbi: Named for the old Kebbi kingdom, whose people the Hausa called the Kabawa.
Argungu in it holds a fishing festival where thousands of men enter the river at once with hand nets and gourds, a truce tradition dating from 1934.
It grows more rice than almost any other state, irrigated from the Niger and the Rima.
jigawa: From a Hausa word for sandy soil, which describes most of it.
Split from Kano in 1991; it is one of the most rural states, with a low urban share and heavy reliance on farming.
The Hadejia river through it supports irrigated rice and wheat in an otherwise dry landscape.
borno: From the Kanem-Bornu empire, one of the longest-lasting states in African history — its dynasty ruled for about a thousand years.
Lake Chad on its border has shrunk by about 90% since the 1960s, which has destroyed fishing and farming livelihoods.
It was the centre of the Boko Haram insurgency from 2009, which displaced over two million people.
kano: Named for the city, traditionally after Kano, a blacksmith who settled at the foot of Dala hill.
The greatest trans-Saharan trade city in Hausaland, walled since the eleventh century, and its dye pits at Kofar Mata have been worked since 1498.
It is the most populous state in northern Nigeria and the commercial capital of the north.
bauchi: Said to be named after a hunter called Baushe who founded the town.
Yankari here is Nigeria's best-known game reserve, with the country's largest surviving elephant population.
Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa, Nigeria's first prime minister, came from this state.
gombe: Named for the town, founded by a Fulani leader in the jihad of the early 1800s.
Split from Bauchi in 1996, one of the last states created.
Its Tangale-Waja hills give it more relief than the plains around, and it sits on the edge of the Sahel.
kaduna: From the Hausa kadduna, plural of kada, "crocodile" — the river was full of them.
The British made it the capital of the Northern Region in 1917, so it is a colonial creation rather than an old emirate.
It sits on the fault line between Muslim north and Christian south, which has made it the site of repeated communal violence.
niger: Named for the river, whose own name probably comes from Tuareg n'ger-n-gereo, "river of rivers" — not from Latin for black.
The largest state in Nigeria by area, and it holds both the Kainji and Shiroro dams.
Gurara falls and the Zuma rock, a 300 m monolith on the Abuja road, are both here.
plateau: Named for the Jos Plateau, which rises to about 1,200 m and is cool enough that the British built a hill station on it.
Tin was mined here from 1902, and the Nok culture nearby produced terracotta sculpture from about 500 BC — the oldest figurative art in West Africa.
Its altitude gives it a climate mild enough to grow strawberries and potatoes in the tropics.
adamawa: Named for Modibbo Adama, the Fulani leader who founded an emirate here in the early 1800s.
The Mandara and Alantika mountains along its Cameroon border hold communities that resisted both the jihad and colonial rule.
Its Sukur cultural landscape, terraced fields and stone-paved paths, is a UNESCO site.
kwara: From a Nupe word for the Niger river.
It is the meeting point of north and south: Yoruba-majority but grouped with the northern states.
Ilorin, its capital, was a Yoruba town taken into the Sokoto Caliphate, which is why it is Muslim-majority and Yoruba-speaking at once.
federal-capital-territory: Not a name but a status: territory carved out in 1976 for a new, neutral capital away from Lagos.
Abuja was chosen for being ethnically neutral and central, and the government moved there in 1991.
Aso Rock, a 400 m monolith, stands behind the presidential complex, which is named after it.
nasarawa: From Arabic nasara, "victory" or "help" — a name given by a nineteenth-century emir.
Split from Plateau in 1996, and it holds a large share of Nigeria's solid minerals, including barite and lithium.
Its Farin Ruwa falls drop about 150 m, among the highest in the country.
oyo: Named for the Oyo Empire, the dominant Yoruba power from the 1600s to the 1830s, with a cavalry that controlled the savanna.
Ibadan, its capital, was the largest city in tropical Africa for much of the twentieth century, and has Nigeria's oldest university, from 1948.
The Old Oyo capital's fall in the 1830s scattered Yoruba people south and is the origin of many modern Yoruba towns.
taraba: The Mambilla Plateau in it is the highest land in Nigeria, above 1,800 m, with tea plantations and a temperate climate.
It is one of the most ethnically diverse states in the country, with dozens of small language groups.
ekiti: From the Yoruba okiti, "hill" — the land of hills, which it is.
It has produced an unusual number of professors for its size, and Nigerians call it the fountain of knowledge.
Ikogosi in it has warm and cold springs that meet and flow side by side without mixing at once.
kogi: From a Hausa or Nupe word for river — appropriately, since the Niger and the Benue meet at Lokoja, its capital.
Lokoja was the first administrative capital of colonial Nigeria, chosen for that confluence.
The state borders ten others, more than any other in Nigeria.
osun: Named for the Osun river and the goddess of the same name.
The Osun-Osogbo sacred grove is a UNESCO site — one of the last intact forest shrines of the Yoruba religion, restored by an Austrian artist who settled there.
Ile-Ife in it is where Yoruba tradition places the creation of the world, and its bronze heads from about 1300 astonished European scholars.
benue: Named for the Benue river, the Niger's largest tributary; the name comes from a Batta phrase, "mother of waters".
Called the food basket of the nation: it produces a large share of Nigeria's yams, and Nigeria grows most of the world's.
The Tiv people here are one of Nigeria's larger groups and were traditionally organised without chiefs.
ogun: Named for the Ogun river, which shares its name with the Yoruba god of iron.
Abeokuta, its capital, means "under the rock", and its Olumo rock sheltered refugees during the nineteenth-century wars.
It has produced more Nigerian heads of state than any other state, including Obasanjo, and Fela Kuti was born here.
ondo: Named for the town of Ondo, whose own name is said to mean "the settlers".
Nigeria's largest cocoa producer, and cocoa was the country's main export before oil.
Idanre hills in it are a UNESCO tentative site, with an old town on top reached by 660 steps.
edo: Named for the Edo people and the Benin Kingdom, whose own capital they called Edo.
The Benin Bronzes were looted from its royal palace by a British expedition in 1897 and are now the most contested objects in European museums.
The Walls of Benin were once among the longest earthworks in the world, several times the length of the Great Wall by some estimates.
lagos: Portuguese for "lakes", after the lagoons — named by traders for the town of Lagos in Portugal.
The smallest state by area and the largest by population, and one of the fastest-growing cities in the world.
It was Nigeria's capital until 1991 and remains its commercial centre; Nollywood, the world's second-largest film industry by output, is based here.
enugu: From Igbo enu ugwu, "the top of the hill".
Coal was found here in 1909 and the city grew around it — it is still called the coal city.
It was the capital of Biafra at the start of the 1967–70 war.
anambra: An anglicised form of Oma Mbala, the name of a tributary of the Niger.
Igbo-Ukwu here produced bronze castings from the ninth century, made by lost-wax methods, centuries before Benin or Ife.
It has one of the highest population densities in Africa and is known for its trading and apprenticeship system.
ebonyi: From Aboine, a river, rendered into English as Ebonyi.
Created in 1996, and it produces most of Nigeria's rice and its salt — Abakaliki is called the salt of the nation.
Its lead and zinc deposits have been mined since colonial times.
cross-river: Named in English for the Cross River, which the Efik called the Oyono.
Calabar was a major slave-trade port and later the first capital of the Niger Coast Protectorate.
Its rainforest holds the Cross River gorilla, the rarest great ape in the world, with about 300 left.
delta: Named for the Niger Delta, one of the largest river deltas in the world.
It produces a large share of Nigeria's oil, and the pollution and gas flaring here have been the subject of international litigation.
Its mangroves are the most extensive in Africa, and the delta has over 240 fish species.
imo: The Aba Women's War of 1929 started in this region — thousands of women protested colonial taxation and forced policy change.
It is one of the most densely populated states, and heavy gully erosion is a serious problem in its soils.
abia: An acronym, unusually: from the initials of Aba, Bende, Isuikwuato and Afikpo, the districts that formed it in 1991.
Aba is Nigeria's informal manufacturing capital, where workshops make shoes and clothing exported across West Africa.
The Long Juju of Arochukwu here was an oracle that arbitrated disputes across Igboland and was used to supply the slave trade.
rivers: Named in English for the many creeks and rivers of the delta it sits in.
Port Harcourt, its capital, is the centre of Nigeria's oil industry and was built by the British in 1913 to export coal from Enugu.
Ken Saro-Wiwa, executed in 1995 for leading Ogoni protests against oil pollution here, made the region an international cause.
akwa-ibom: From the Qua Iboe river, rendered in Ibibio as Akwa Ibom.
It has one of the highest oil outputs in the country, and Ibom is the largest ethnic group, the Ibibio.
Its Ibeno beach is one of the longest sand beaches in West Africa.
bayelsa: Another acronym: Brass, Yenagoa and Sagbama, the three areas joined to make it in 1996.
The smallest state by population, and almost entirely creeks, swamp and mangrove — much of it is reachable only by boat.
Oloibiri in it is where Nigerian oil was first struck in 1956; the well is dry and the town has little to show for it.
nguru: Of Kanuri origin; the town was a trading post of the Bornu empire.
Its wetlands, where the Hadejia and Jama’are rivers meet, are a vital stop for birds crossing the Sahara.
It was the northern terminus of the colonial railway branch built to carry groundnuts.
gashua: It sits on the Yobe river, which forms part of the border with Niger.
It is a market town for the Bade and Kanuri, in the Sahel scrub.
birnin-kebbi: "The walled city of Kebbi" — birnin is a Hausa word for a walled town.
It was the capital of the Kebbi kingdom, which held out against the Songhai empire.
Argungu nearby holds a fishing festival where thousands enter the river at once with hand nets.
gusau: Named for a founder or a local family.
It grew as a cotton and groundnut trading centre after the railway reached it in 1929.
It is the capital of Zamfara, the first Nigerian state to adopt sharia criminal law.
maiduguri: From a Kanuri phrase, possibly "the place where one learns" or a founder’s name.
It was founded in 1907 as the British headquarters for Bornu, replacing the older capital at Kukawa.
It became the centre of the Boko Haram insurgency from 2009 and has absorbed hundreds of thousands of displaced people.
damaturu: The capital of Yobe, made a state capital only in 1991.
It sits on the road between Maiduguri and Kano, the main route across the north-east.
funtua: It is one of the main cotton and groundnut markets of the north-west.
It has a textile mill and lies on the railway from Lagos to Kano.
bama: Of Kanuri origin; the town was a district capital of the Bornu empire.
It was one of the towns worst affected by the insurgency and was largely destroyed.
It sits on the road towards Cameroon, near the Sambisa forest.
zaria: Named for Zaria, a daughter of a queen of Zazzau — the older name of the city-state.
Queen Amina, her sister, is credited with the walls that surround many Hausa towns.
Ahmadu Bello University here is one of the largest in Africa.
mubi: Of local origin, in the Adamawa hills.
It is a major cattle market on the Cameroon border.
The Mandara mountains beside it hold communities that resisted both the Fulani jihad and colonial rule.
jos: Possibly a corruption of Gwosh, a local village name, misheard by the British.
It sits at about 1,200 m, cool enough that the British built a hill station there.
The Nok culture nearby produced terracotta sculpture from about 500 BC, the oldest figurative art in West Africa.
minna: Two Nigerian heads of state, Babangida and Abubakar, came from this town.
It is a rail junction and the capital of Niger state, Nigeria’s largest by area.
bida: Of Nupe origin; it was the capital of the Nupe kingdom.
Its glassmakers and brass workers use techniques passed down through families for centuries.
Nupe glass beads made here were traded across West Africa.
abuja: Named for an older town, now called Suleja, whose emir was called Abuja.
Built from nothing after 1976 as a neutral capital, and the government moved in 1991.
Aso Rock, a 400 m monolith, stands behind the presidential complex and gives it its name.
jalingo: The capital of Taraba, one of Nigeria’s most ethnically diverse states.
The Mambilla Plateau in its state is the highest land in Nigeria, with tea plantations at 1,800 m.
ilorin: From a Yoruba phrase about sharpening iron on stone — ilu erin, or a variant.
It is a Yoruba town that was taken into the Sokoto Caliphate, which is why it is Muslim-majority and Yoruba-speaking at once.
Its pottery and aso oke weaving are both long-established crafts.
lafia: The capital of Nasarawa, created in 1996.
The state holds a large share of Nigeria’s barite and lithium deposits.
ogbomoso: Named for Ogunlola, a hunter who killed a marauder called Elemoso — "Ogun ta Elemoso".
It has one of the largest Nigerian diasporas in the United States relative to its size.
It is a major yam and cassava market in Oyo state.
osogbo: From a phrase about the goddess Osun — "oso igbo", the wizard of the forest.
Its sacred grove is a UNESCO site, one of the last intact forest shrines of the Yoruba religion.
An Austrian artist, Susanne Wenger, settled there and spent decades restoring its shrines.
makurdi: It sits on the Benue, and its bridge is one of the few crossings of that river.
It is the capital of Benue, called the food basket of the nation for its yams.
ado-ekiti: "The camp of Ekiti" — ado means a camp or settlement, Ekiti the land of hills.
It is the capital of Ekiti, a state that has produced an unusual number of professors for its size.
Its Ewi is one of the senior traditional rulers of Yorubaland.
iwo: Its Oluwo is a traditional ruler whose title dates from the sixteenth century.
It is a farming town in Osun state, growing cocoa and kola nut.
ikare: Of Yoruba origin, in the Akoko district.
It sits among granite inselbergs on the border between Ondo and Kogi.
It is a market town at the meeting point of Yoruba, Edo and Ebira territory.
ife: Ile-Ife means "the house of expansion" — Yoruba tradition places the creation of the world here.
Its bronze and terracotta heads from about 1300 are among the finest naturalistic sculpture ever made in Africa.
When Europeans first saw them they refused to believe Africans had made them, and invented theories about Greeks.
ibadan: From eba odan, "by the edge of the savanna" — where forest meets grassland.
It was the largest city in tropical Africa for much of the twentieth century.
Nigeria’s oldest university opened here in 1948, and Wole Soyinka and Chinua Achebe both studied there.
akure: Of Yoruba origin, possibly from a phrase about a king’s beads breaking.
The capital of Ondo, Nigeria’s largest cocoa-producing state.
The Idanre hills nearby hold an old town on top, reached by 660 steps.
owo: Its museum holds terracotta sculpture that links the art of Ife and Benin.
Its palace was said to be the largest in Africa, with over a hundred courtyards.
abeokuta: "Under the rock" — abe under, okuta a rock, for the Olumo rock that sheltered refugees.
That refuge was from the nineteenth-century Yoruba wars, and the rock is still climbed.
Fela Kuti was born here, and it has produced more Nigerian heads of state than any other town.
nsukka: The University of Nigeria here, opened 1960, was the country’s first fully indigenous university.
Chinua Achebe taught there, and it was overrun early in the Biafran war.
ijebu-ode: "Ijebu of the outer part" — the capital of the Ijebu kingdom.
That kingdom controlled the trade routes to Lagos and resisted the British until 1892.
Its Ojude Oba festival, three days after Eid, parades age-grade groups on horseback.
benin-city: From the kingdom of Benin — unconnected to the modern Republic of Benin next door, which borrowed the name in 1975.
The Benin Bronzes were looted from its royal palace by a British expedition in 1897.
Its Walls of Benin were once among the longest earthworks in the world, several times the length of the Great Wall by some estimates.
awka: Of Igbo origin, linked to blacksmithing — its smiths travelled across Igboland.
It is the capital of Anambra.
Igbo-Ukwu nearby produced bronze castings from the ninth century, centuries before Benin or Ife.
sapele: From the name of a local tree, which gives its name to sapele mahogany.
That timber has been exported to Europe for furniture and veneer for over a century.
It was a major Niger Delta river port for rubber and palm oil.
umuahia: "The children of Ahia" — umu is a common Igbo prefix meaning the children or people of.
It was the capital of Biafra after Enugu fell in 1967.
The Ojukwu bunker and the war museum there preserve that period.
warri: From Iwere, the name of the Itsekiri kingdom.
The Portuguese traded here from the 1480s, and an Itsekiri prince was educated in Portugal in the 1600s.
It is a centre of the oil industry and one of the most ethnically mixed delta towns.
owerri: It is called the entertainment capital of eastern Nigeria for its hotels and nightlife.
It was the last capital of Biafra before the war ended in January 1970.
aba: Its workshops make shoes and clothing exported across West Africa, which is why it is called Nigeria’s Japan.
The Aba Women’s War of 1929 started here — thousands of women protested colonial taxation and forced a policy change.
uyo: The capital of Akwa Ibom, one of Nigeria’s main oil-producing states.
Its stadium, built in 2014, is one of the best-regarded in the country.
calabar: Possibly from the Portuguese calabar, or from an Efik phrase; the river was the Calabar.
It was a major slave-trade port and later the first capital of the Niger Coast Protectorate.
Its month-long December carnival is the largest street party in Africa.
port-harcourt: Named in 1913 for Lewis Harcourt, the British colonial secretary, who did not want the honour.
It was built to ship coal from Enugu and became the centre of Nigeria’s oil industry.
Ken Saro-Wiwa, executed in 1995 for leading Ogoni protests against oil pollution, was tried here.
